candidates.title: Proceedings from the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections: the definition of Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint infection.
candidates.authors_short: Namdari S, Zmistowski B, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains one of the greatest diagnostic and treatment challenges facing shoulder surgeons and their patients. A definition for shoulder PJI was established by the 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) on Orthopedic Infections, but the selection and weighting of its minor criteria relied largely on expert opinion. The purpose of this study was to present an updated, evidence-based definition of shoulder PJI generated by the 2025 ICM Shoulder Group. METHODS: The 2025 ICM Shoulder Group, an international panel of shoulder surgeons and infectious disease specialists, used a modified Delphi process informed by 86 systematic reviews and by a predictive statistical model derived from the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Multicenter Revision Arthroplasty and PJI Group dataset to reconsider the 2018 ICM definition of shoulder PJI, including its major criteria, minor criteria, and diagnostic categories. RESULTS: The delegates voted to eliminate organism virulence from the definition and to retain gross intra-articular purulence and presence of a sinus tract as the two criteria defining Definite PJI. The Minor Criteria were revised to include erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), elevated synovial neutrophil percentage, positive frozen section, radiographic humeral osteolysis, intraoperative humeral loosening, and positive culture, each statistically weighted using the predictive model. Non-definite PJI was categorized by summed minor criteria score as High likelihood (≥13 points), Moderate likelihood (7-12 points), Unknown (1-6 points), or No PJI (0 points). The final definition achieved unanimous delegate consensus (51 of 51 delegates; 100% agreement; super majority, strong consensus). CONCLUSIONS: The 2025 ICM definition of shoulder PJI represents an evidence-informed evolution of the 2018 definition, combining statistical modeling of prospective multicenter data with structured expert consensus. The definition is expected to continue to evolve as further shoulder-specific data become available.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality consensus proceedings from the 2025 ICM with international expert panel using systematic review methodology to update the shoulder PJI definition—directly applicable to all shoulder arthroplasty surgeons managing infection.
bullets: The 2025 ICM updated the shoulder PJI definition, keeping purulence and sinus tract as definite PJI criteria while removing organism virulence from the scoring system.

A weighted minor criteria scoring system now categorizes non-definite cases as high likelihood (13+ points), moderate likelihood (7-12), unknown (1-6), or no PJI (0), using ESR, CRP, synovial neutrophil percentage, frozen section, osteolysis, loosening, and culture results.
Shoulder surgeons evaluating revision arthroplasty patients now have an evidence-based, statistically derived diagnostic framework to guide PJI workup and treatment decisions.

candidates.title: Defining Long-Term Success After Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty: Survivorship and Clinically Important Outcomes.
candidates.authors_short: Kucharik MP, Hung V, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term success after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA) is frequently defined by implant survivorship, but revision-free survival may not reflect durable clinical benefit. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 791 consecutive aTSAs performed between 2003 and 2015 was conducted. Implant survivorship was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Clinical outcomes were evaluated at a 10-year landmark, and clinically important thresholds for the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score were derived using patient satisfaction as the anchor. Multivariable regression identified predictors of revision and substantial clinical benefit (SCB). RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier survivorship was 96.1% at 10 years and 93.7% at 15 years. Walch B glenoid morphology and younger age were independently associated with revision. Clinical outcomes remained improved at long-term follow-up despite gradual attenuation over time. At 10 years, the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) threshold for the ASES score was 68.1, and 69.5% of shoulders achieved it. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and SCB thresholds for the change in ASES score were 14.0 and 39.2, achieved by 79.9% and 55.8% of shoulders, respectively. Younger age, primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and lower preoperative ASES score were independently associated with achievement of SCB. CONCLUSIONS: aTSA demonstrated excellent long-term implant survivorship and modest patient-reported outcomes, although shoulder function gradually attenuated over extended follow-up. Despite the gradual functional decline, most patients maintained clinically meaningful benefit at 10 years. Younger age and Walch B morphology increased revision risk. Long-term clinically important thresholds provide patient-centered benchmarks for defining durable success. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective cohort (791 aTSAs) in JBJS defining long-term survivorship, MCID/SCB/PASS thresholds, and predictors of revision and clinical benefit for anatomic TSA—highly clinically actionable with excellent sample size.
bullets: Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty shows 96% implant survival at 10 years and 94% at 15 years, but about 30% of patients do not reach an acceptable symptom state by the 10-year mark.
Younger patients and those with Walch B glenoid morphology face higher revision risk and should be counseled accordingly before surgery.
Functional gains after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty gradually decline over time, so long-term follow-up and realistic patient expectations are essential parts of preoperative planning.

candidates.title: Differences in valgus and internal-rotation instability after sequential distal ulnar collateral ligament release: a cadaveric study using Thiel-embalmed cadavers.
candidates.authors_short: Matsuzawa K, Edama M, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Distal ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) tears in overhead athletes have poorer outcomes with conservative treatment than proximal tears, potentially because of limited vascularity and altered ulnohumeral alignment. Previous in vivo studies have demonstrated excessive internal rotation malalignment in distal UCL tears. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether distal tears produce greater internal rotation instability compared with valgus instability. This cadaveric study aimed to quantify valgus and internal rotation instabilities after sequential distal UCL tears using ultrasonography in Thiel-embalmed cadavers. METHODS: Twelve elbows from six Thiel-embalmed cadavers were evaluated. A distal UCL tear model was created by sequentially releasing the distal footprint of the anterior bundle: intact, 5 mm release (partial tear), and approximately 10 mm release (complete tear). Valgus instability was assessed by measuring the medial joint space (MJS) with the elbow at 90° flexion under a 1 kg valgus load. Internal rotation instability was quantified by measuring the posteromedial joint space (PMJS) with the forearm maximally pronated under the same load. Three images per condition were obtained, and mean values were analyzed. The rate of change in MJS and PMJS was calculated by dividing the MJS or PMJS value (mm) under each UCL-release condition by the corresponding value in the intact condition. The resulting rate of change was unitless. Conditions were compared using one-way analysis of variance with Bonferroni correction, paired t-tests with P values adjusted using the Holm method were used to compare the rates of change between MJS and PMJS. RESULTS: MJS and PMJS increased significantly from intact to partial and complete tears (all P < .01), with effect sizes >0.8. PMJS showed a significantly greater rate of change than MJS in both partial tears (1.46 ± 0.17 vs 1.29 ± 0.19; P = .018) and complete tears (1.94 ± 0.33 vs 1.65 ± 0.21; P = .018). CONCLUSION: Distal UCL tears increased both valgus and internal rotation instability; however, internal rotation instability increased more. Therefore, functional factors, particularly increased internal rotation instability, may contribute to the characteristic internal rotation malalignment and poor prognosis of distal UCL tears. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Basic Science Study, Biomechanics.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large population-based cohort of 3,159 patients comparing ORIF vs RHA for radial head fractures with long follow-up, providing strong evidence that RHA has lower reoperation rates—directly actionable for upper extremity surgeons.
bullets: Cutting the distal UCL in cadaver elbows increased both valgus and internal rotation instability, but internal rotation instability increased more than valgus instability.
This applies to overhead athletes with distal UCL tears, who tend to do worse with conservative treatment than those with proximal tears.
The greater internal rotation instability from distal tears likely explains the rotational malalignment seen clinically and may justify more aggressive surgical decision-making for this tear pattern.

candidates.title: Cemented Femoral Fixation for Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty in the United States: How Surgeon-Cemented Volume Impacts Failure Risk.
candidates.authors_short: Abrolat JL, Zedan AM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although cementless femoral fixation remains the United States (U.S.) standard, recent data shows a decline in exclusive cementless usage from 34 to 14% between 2018 and 2024. Whether surgeon-cemented total hip arthroplasty (THA) volume affects implant survivorship remains unclear in this traditionally low-volume environment. As such, we evaluated the association between surgeon cemented stem volume and risk of all-cause revision. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used a national database to identify primary THAs with cemented femoral fixation from 2016 to 2020. Surgeons were classified by their five-year cemented stem volume: Group 1 (less than 60 stems) or Group 2 (≥ 60 stems). Patients had a minimum two-year follow-up and were propensity score-matched 1:1 based on demographics and comorbidities. A total of 7,174 matched patients were analyzed (3,587 per cohort). Outcomes were all-cause revision, periprosthetic fracture (PPF), mechanical loosening, periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), and dislocation within five years. RESULTS: Patients treated by Group 1 surgeons had higher rates of all study outcomes. At two years, Group 1 patients had higher odds of all-cause revision (odds ratio (OR) = 2.10; 95% confidence interval: 1.44 to 3.11; P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed revision risk diverged sharply within the first postoperative year and persisted through five years. At two-year follow-up, Group 1 patients had increased risk of PPF (OR = 1.58; P = 0.038), loosening (OR = 2.21; P < 0.001), PJI (OR = 2.19; P < 0.001), and dislocation (OR = 2.51; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Low surgeon cemented stem volume is strongly associated with increased risk of revision following cemented THA. While cemented femoral fixation remains a useful alternative for high-risk patients undergoing elective THA, the benefits may be compromised if the surgery is performed by surgeons whose specific volume for this type of fixation is low.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large national database study (72,672 matched patients) examining RCRI, individual risk factor duration, and age strata on MACE after TKA—highly clinically relevant for preoperative risk stratification in arthroplasty practice.
bullets: Surgeons performing fewer than 60 cemented total hip stems over five years had twice the revision rate compared to higher-volume surgeons at two-year follow-up.
Low-volume cemented stem surgeons also had significantly higher rates of periprosthetic fracture, loosening, infection, and dislocation within five years.
When considering a cemented femoral stem in primary total hip arthroplasty, surgeon-specific cemented volume should factor into the decision, particularly for high-risk patients.

candidates.title: Mechanical Failure and Revision Risk Following Transition from PFNA to TFNA: A Single-Center Cohort Study of 1,970 Patients.
candidates.authors_short: Ben Zoor I, Fogel I, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, and time to failure between two cephalomedullary nail designs following an institutional transition. METHODS: Design: Retrospective consecutive cohort study. SETTING: Single Level I trauma center, Israel. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged >65 years with acute OTA/AO 31A fractures (subtypes 31A1-31A3) treated with a short cephalomedullary nail with helical blade fixation, either the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) or the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA), between January 2018 and May 2025 were included. Implant type was determined solely by an institutional transition from PFNA to TFNA in March 2023 for logistical reasons rather than surgeon preference. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, time to failure, body mass index (BMI), and Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) were compared between groups. Mortality within the early revision-risk window was compared between groups to exclude survival bias. RESULTS: The PFNA cohort comprised 1,388 patients (mean age 83.1 years, range 65-102; 986 females [71.0%]) and the TFNA cohort 582 patients (mean age 82.9 years, range 65-107; 407 females [69.9%]); baseline demographics were comparable (age, p=0.691; sex, p=0.626). Orthopedic follow-up was 63.9% for the TFNA cohort versus 61.0% for the PFNA cohort (p=0.24), with a shorter maximum observation period for TFNA (TFNA 26 vs. PFNA 88 months).TFNA was associated with a five-fold increase in implant mechanical failure relative to PFNA (TFNA 1.6% vs. PFNA 0.3%; RR=5.36, 95% CI 1.66-17.3; p=0.005), primarily driven by a four-fold increase in cut-outs (1.2% vs. 0.3%; RR=4.18, 95% CI 1.23-14.2; p=0.027). Failures occurred earlier with TFNA (median 80.0 vs. 244.0 days; p=0.027). Among cut-outs, OTA/AO subtype distribution did not differ (31A1: TFNA 57.1% vs. PFNA 50.0%; no 31A3 in either group; p=1.00); TFNA patients had a higher BMI (median 23.9 vs. 20.1 kg/m2; p=0.024), but mean TAD did not differ (TFNA 24.6 vs. PFNA 21.1 mm; p=0.37). Mortality within the revision-risk window did not differ (TFNA 7.2% vs. PFNA 8.8%; p=0.24). CONCLUSIONS: The transition to the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA) was associated with five-fold higher mechanical failure and four-fold higher cut-out rates than the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) with earlier failures suggesting reduced mechanical stability of the TFNA during early fracture healing. Heightened vigilance is warranted when using TFNA, particularly in patients with higher body mass index early postoperatively. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large single-center cohort of 1,970 patients comparing PFNA vs TFNA cephalomedullary nails in elderly hip fracture patients with near-identical demographics, finding fivefold difference in mechanical failure—directly practice-changing for trauma surgeons.
bullets: In elderly hip fracture patients treated with short cephalomedullary nails, the TFNA had five times more mechanical failures and four times more screw cut-outs than the PFNA.
Failures with the TFNA occurred much earlier after surgery (median 80 days vs. 244 days), and higher BMI patients who received TFNA were overrepresented among cut-outs.
Surgeons using the TFNA for intertrochanteric fractures should follow patients closely in the first three months, especially if the patient is heavier or blade position is not ideal.

candidates.title: Letter to the Editor Regarding "Maternal and Fetal Perioperative Outcomes After Pelvic Ring or Acetabulum Fracture in Gravid Patients".
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective RCT comparing ORIF early vs delayed weight bearing after syndesmotic fixation with suture button, published in JOT—high study design quality addressing a common clinical question though limited by small sample size.
bullets: This letter responds to a study on pelvic ring and acetabulum fractures repaired surgically in pregnant patients, raising methodological concerns about the original findings.
The population in question is pregnant trauma patients requiring orthopaedic fixation, a rare but high-stakes group where both maternal and fetal outcomes are at risk.
Surgeons treating gravid patients with pelvic fractures should interpret the original study's perioperative outcome data with caution until the raised concerns are addressed.

candidates.title: Letting the Patient Lead: Weightbearing to Tolerance and the Evolving Science of Recovery After First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Fusion.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective RCT of 68 patients comparing immediate weightbearing vs non-weightbearing after first MTP fusion in Foot & Ankle International—high study design quality and directly applicable to foot and ankle surgical practice.
bullets: First metatarsophalangeal joint fusion patients can bear weight as tolerated postoperatively without increased rates of nonunion or complications.
This approach applies to standard first MTP fusion candidates across foot and ankle orthopaedic practice.
Surgeons can move away from prolonged non-weightbearing protocols, which improves patient recovery experience without compromising bone healing.

candidates.title: Systemic Exposure and Renal Safety After Intrawound Vancomycin Powder in Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Prospective Comparative Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: Bingol O, Karlidag T, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Intrawound vancomycin powder has been proposed as a local prophylactic measure, but concerns remain regarding systemic absorption and nephrotoxicity. This study evaluated systemic absorption, renal safety, and postoperative infection outcomes after intrawound vancomycin use in primary TKA. METHODS: This prospective comparative cohort study included 260 patients who underwent primary TKA at a single tertiary care center: 130 in the vancomycin cohort and 130 in the control cohort. The vancomycin cohort received one gram of intrawound vancomycin powder before closure. Serum vancomycin levels were measured 12 hours postoperatively. Serial renal function and kidney disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO)-defined acute kidney injury (AKI) was analyzed in all patients. Infection and wound-complication outcomes were assessed in patients who completed at least six months of follow-up. RESULTS: The 12-hour serum vancomycin levels were below the laboratory reporting threshold (less than 1.00 mg/L) in 104 of 130 patients (80.0%). Among the remaining 26 patients who had numerical values, the median concentration was 0.28 mg/L (interquartile range [IQR], 0.21 to 1.26; range, 0.01 to 2.76 mg/L), which was well below systemic therapeutic levels. Serum vancomycin concentration was not correlated with early changes in serum creatinine or estimated glomerular filtration rate (Spearman ρ range, -0.08 to -0.03; all P ≥ 0.720). AKI occurred in nine patients (6.9%) in the vancomycin group and eight patients (6.2%) in the control group (odds ratio, 1.13; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.42 to 3.04; P = 1.000). All AKI events in the vancomycin group were stage 1. Surgery-related complication rates were similar between groups, with no statistically significant differences in PJI, superficial infection, or wound dehiscence. CONCLUSION: Intrawound administration of one gram of vancomycin powder in primary TKA resulted in minimal systemic exposure and showed no clinically meaningful nephrotoxicity signal. However, it was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in infection or wound-complication outcomes; therefore, these data do not support its routine prophylactic use in primary TKA.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective RCT in JBJS comparing bi-unicompartmental vs cruciate-retaining TKA for bicompartmental OA showing no clinical difference in FJS at 24 months—important randomized evidence for knee arthroplasty surgeons evaluating UKA alternatives.
bullets: One gram of intrawound vancomycin powder in primary TKA produces minimal systemic absorption, with serum levels undetectable in 80% of patients at 12 hours.
Kidney injury rates were identical between vancomycin and control groups, so nephrotoxicity is not a reason to avoid local vancomycin in routine TKA patients.
Despite renal safety, vancomycin powder did not reduce infection or wound complications, so this study does not support its routine use in primary TKA.

candidates.title: Meniscal Root Tears: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Management, and Outcomes.
candidates.authors_short: Livingston M, Ross P, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: ➢ Meniscal root tears compromise load distribution within the knee, accelerating cartilage degeneration and leading to knee osteoarthritis.➢ Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion supported by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), with arthroscopy serving as the gold standard for confirmation.➢ Management decisions should be tailored to patient-specific factors, including age, activity level, tear characteristics, and the severity of degenerative chondral wear evident on preoperative imaging, including weight-bearing radiographs and MRI.➢ Root repair is associated with better long-term outcomes compared with partial meniscectomy and nonoperative management in appropriately selected patients.➢ There is currently no universally accepted postoperative rehabilitation protocol following meniscal root repair; however, most strategies limit weight-bearing in the early postoperative period and restrict loaded flexion, such as deep squatting, for up to 4 to 5 months. Further research is needed to guide standardized recovery pathways.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS current concepts review on meniscal root tears covering epidemiology, diagnosis, management, and outcomes—comprehensive and directly applicable to sports and general orthopaedic surgeons managing a frequently encountered and consequential injury.
bullets: Meniscal root tears disrupt knee load distribution and accelerate cartilage loss, progressing to osteoarthritis if untreated.
In appropriately selected patients, root repair produces better long-term outcomes than partial meniscectomy or nonoperative management.
Most postoperative protocols restrict weight-bearing early and limit loaded knee flexion for up to 4 to 5 months, though no standardized rehabilitation pathway exists yet.

candidates.title: Payment Model Evolution for Spinal Fusions.
candidates.authors_short: Rubin I, Bruggeman A, Bozic KJ
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: Value-based payment reform in the United States is rapidly evolving, with new models from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services targeting a range of inpatient and outpatient procedures. To trace this evolution, we examine spinal fusion-a procedure consistently included in past and emerging models-as a lens to compare model characteristics, payment structure, quality measurement, and primary care integration. We analyze Bundled Payments for Care Improvement-Advanced (BPCI-A, 2018 to 2025), Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM, launched in 2026), Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions (ACCESS, launching in July 2026), Ambulatory Specialty Model (ASM, launching in 2027), and proposed condition-based bundled payments. BPCI-A laid the groundwork for bundled spinal fusion payments but was voluntary and lacked integration with primary care. TEAM and ASM mandate participation from inpatient and outpatient specialists, respectively; TEAM also requires primary care referrals after discharge. ACCESS incorporates technology tools into specialty care, while condition-based bundles embed specialty care within Accountable Care Organizations; both prioritize longitudinal care integration. We conclude that future reforms should combine aspects of the aforementioned models, prioritizing primary care-specialist collaboration, integration of acute and chronic care pathways, and quality metrics that reflect patient outcomes.
candidates.score_reasoning: Systematic review and meta-analysis in JBJS on cemented femoral fixation volume-outcome relationship using a national database of 7,174 matched THA patients—important for credentialing, training, and policy decisions around cemented THA.
bullets: CMS has launched or is launching four payment models covering spinal fusion from 2026 onward, moving from the voluntary BPCI-A bundle toward mandatory participation for both inpatient and outpatient spine specialists.
Newer models require primary care involvement after discharge and link specialty spine care to chronic disease management, shifting accountability beyond the surgical episode itself.

Orthopaedic spine surgeons should expect mandatory bundled payment participation, increased coordination requirements with primary care, and quality metrics tied to patient outcomes rather than process measures.
